why: The Rust bundler and the JavaScript compiler each expand import.meta.glob. Both must produce the same matches, the same key order, and the same lowering, or a route behaves differently in dev, SSG, and production. Version 1 of this fixture only ever declared cases with zero or one match, so it asserted the word 'deterministic' without ever exercising an order, and the two implementations silently disagreed.

cases.name: lazy relative nested matches, including the zero-directory case

ordering.why: Keys are ordered by slash-normalized code units, never by locale collation. localeCompare orders 'beta.ts' before 'Gamma.ts' and varies with the host ICU locale; code-unit order puts every uppercase initial first and is identical on every machine. These names differ by more than case so the fixture also runs on case-insensitive filesystems.

matching.why: `**/` stands for zero or more whole path segments. Both expanders used to let it consume the value one character at a time, so `./posts/**/index.mdx` matched `./posts/notindex.mdx` — `**/` swallowed `not` and the rest matched literally — and `./posts/**/b/*.mdx` reached into `./posts/ab/`. Each pattern is expanded against `files` and must produce exactly `expected`, in code-unit order.

symlinks.why: A symbolic link is never followed and never matched, whether it names a file or a directory. The JavaScript expander walks with Dirent.isDirectory()/isFile(), both false for a link; the Rust expander asked Path::is_dir(), which follows one, so a linked directory was walked — and its target, possibly outside the project, compiled — by one graph only. Creating a link can need privileges (Windows without Developer Mode), so a replay that cannot create one skips rather than fails.

lowering.why: An eager match must enter the static dependency graph as a namespace import. Emitting require() only worked in the Rust linker, which rewrites it; on the JavaScript graph the same text reached an ES module and threw 'require is not defined'.

scanning.why: import.meta.glob occurrences inside strings, comments, template text, and regular-expression literals are not calls. A regex literal containing a quote, such as /['"]/, is the case that blinded a hand-written scanner: it starts a string skip that runs to the next quote anywhere in the file and swallows the real call.
